title: MV vs. MZ for my next project

posts.author: Blackfield
posts.body:
Hi all,
my first project (Tales of Vogar) was a big success on steam with right now over 1.000 sales. I am currrently in the concept phase for Part 2, which will be professional and not hobby anymore.
Now I am wondering what engine to use. While I am good enough to "program code" in the engine, completely creating new plugins is not my strong suit. Since I will have a certain budget on my hands the question is:
When I contract people to write specific plugins, is there an advantage/disadvantage using one or the other MV/MZ?
I will also have to adjust a lot for the SV battle system. While turn based is not dead, the way it is implemented in the RPG Maker it is. Stuff like (timed) parrying, counter attacks, timed attacks with button input are not standard and are things, that make turn based battles interesting again.
Finally, I wonder about graphics, too. What engine is better for light-plugins? I remember running in some issues with MV and terrax lighting which were not huge, but for a commercial game not good enough.
In the end, it would probably make sense to switch to a different engine for what I want. But I feel like the time spent to learn using that engine compared to what extremely deep knowledge I have for the RPG Maker would be a total waste.
Thanks for your ideas, thoughts and inputs!

posts.author: fizzly
posts.body: Was many topics about this, but in short: pick MZ, it's just MV on steroids, many things was upgraded and implemented as default, so some plugins may not be even necessery. Also, in retrospect, if I were to judge it today, I personally would not have found a solution that was missing in MZ and was present in MV (also having plugins in mind).

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body:
I think it would be worth your time to make a small game or game module in mz to experience the differences, good and bad for yourself.
If you're making games for the long haul, there is no correct answer, except that you should be able to visualize the difference, which requires doing.
Not many developers come on the forum rueing the day they ever started using MZ.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
MZ is more advanced than MV and has had a lot of improvements on it, from manual layer control in mapping to particle-based animations (MV-style animations are also there, but a bit hidden) and more.
the main disadvantage of MZ is that a lot of the plugins are obfuscated by their programmers, making compatibility patches more difficult to impossible to program. But no one forces you to use obfuscated plugins, it is just time-consuming to look for alternatives.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
MZ is mostly the same as MV, so if you're familiar with MV, there shouldn't be much of a learning curve. At an API level (ie, for creating plugins), it's similar enough that many plugins work equally on MV and MZ, sometimes even without any special code to detect the version. The only thing to figure out, then, is whether plugins for the mechanics you want exist for MZ.
For my part, the only reason I'm still using MV is because I started in MV and it feels like too much effort to switch in mid-project. If I started up a brand-new project, I would use MZ.
In short: unless you have some big reason to use MV (for example, there's an absolutely essential plugin that you can't do without that doesn't have an MZ version), I'd say go with MZ.

posts.author: DrFreeman
posts.body:
These are some of the features in MZ:
https://www.rpgmakerweb.com/products/rpg-maker-mz
This is a review of the features in 3 minutes
You might need to compare the advantages and disadvantages of the purchase.
You'll have to ask yourself, what is the price break point where you need or want to buy it? If you needed a rogue-like element and it is going to take you about 40 hours to make, it would be better to upgrade to MZ. Normally, RPG Maker MZ is $80, but you can
get it on sale now for about $34 on Steam
. That would put development time at less than $1 per hour. If you needed one of the new commands, upgrade. If you were coming from an older version of RPG Maker (where we worried about our palette selection), I would highly recommend upgrading. Shaders are easier on MZ than MV to me. There might be a roundabout way to make it easier, but out of the box, it seems easier on MZ.
From my perspective, there is a significant amount of more plugins in MV than MZ. But MZ development often follows current trends. There are tools to transition projects and plugins over. Since you have a finished product already, you could experience a migration. Some are easier than others.
For me, developing plugins is easier on MZ than MV, but that's my personal experience. Ports used to be easier on MV than MZ, but consoles have moved on to other things and we also have applications to help port on the forums like iOS/MacOSX. Sometimes I'm a bit surprised I don't seen RPG Maker games in the SnapStore on Linux or the Microsoft Store.
What are your objectives, requirements, and specifications?
How does RPG Maker MV fulfill that?
How would RPG Maker MZ fulfill it?
The choice up to you.

Click to expand...
Yes, my recommendation was if they wanted to make an (2D turn-based, grid-based) RPG stick with RPG Maker. Whether it's worth switching to another engine depends on how much of another genre's gameplay the OP plans to have.
The RPG Maker devs themselves peddled Godot by making Action Game Maker; they tied the future of the company to Godot (right after doing the same with Unity) and require that their customers use Godot to use their new product. AGM supposedly reduces/eliminates the need for coding (alternatively the free Orchestrator add-on) so you can even support the RPG Maker devs while using Godot if you want.
"Designing from scratch" sounds scary until you realize that also means you have complete control to make things look and work exactly how you want. Other engines are built to support creating scenes from scratch and have an abundance of tools in the engine to make it easy. RPG Maker is built to provide you with premade scene templates with a lot more limited customization, which is why you often hear "All RPG Maker games look, play and feel the same".
Another thing to keep in mind is other engines get updated far more often than RPG Maker, meaning the gap between what they can do vs RPG Maker increases over time, and subsequently the technical gap between your game and your competitors' games made in other engines.

posts.author: Blackfield
posts.body:
Wow thank you all for the great input! No idea where to start with my answer so sorry if it is a bit unorganized:
Long story short: I believe I will stick to MV. The only upside for me I see is the 3D particle effects. Layers are not my concern as I do parallax mapping only and the rest can be substituted with plugins.
My biggest problem with MZ is I think the community support / plugins. When I was looking for MZ plugin threads there were often none that could give me an answer to my question - it feels like not too many devs switched to MZ or the community itself is just getting smaller. Especially when it comes to compatibility issues between plugins late in development, an information I could have found earlier if others had issues as well, feels like a huge risk to me.
Side note from the "financial view": I wouldn't care to spend (up to) 500 USD to get all the plugins for MZ that I need. The new project will have a budget for that. But again, I feel like the risk of incompatibility is bigger than the reward of particle effects.
One last question about how you feel about particle effects:
A publisher I am in contact with said that the new game needs to be cohesive in its looks. For example I used dragonbones SV battlers as enemies and my heroes were "pixel art". Would you think that 3D particles would also interrupt the 2D pixel art feeling? In my opinion yes, which would be the final argument not to use MZ.

posts.author: Eden019
posts.body:
MZ
- Better quality of life (built-in ATB, change fonts, resolution options)
- Map layers
- Easier eventing (move event preview is really good)
- Just like Aerosys, MZ Plugin command will make your plugin command less hassle.
- Slightly better RTP music
- Lesser choices of community made plugins, and also obfuscated & paid plugins.
MV
- Better RTP tileset, sprites and facesets
- A lot of free plugins , cheaper plugins & not obfuscated!
- IMO, The Animation is better, personally I don't like Effekseer (it looks like too "built-in"), I always like frame per frame animations..
Personally, I wanted to use MZ for my 2nd project, and eventually I decided to go back to MV again because of a plugin I want is not available in MZ yet.
Though , we cannot decide if one day MZ will have more plugins than MV, we'll see...

So I did some research, spend a few bucks and it looks like it comes down to these two:
1) I use visustella and have to 100% rely on their staff for support because you cannot edit the code (hence support questions in the forum often end with the same argument).

I feel like the situation for MV was a little different. Most people used the basis of yanfly, stuff from SRdude/galve and others were pretty much always "built" to work with yanfly. Rarely you had some interoperability issues between the two.

I feel like that is only the tip of the iceberg...

posts.author: rpgLord69
posts.body: You can put your timed dodges/parries and timed attacks in the VS action sequences. Just don't use 'wait for movement' etc + put a loop checking for input trigger and break the loop after x frames. Maybe you can play with the MECH: Once Parallel common events too. VS Action Sequence Impact also gives action sequence commands for Time Stop and Time Scale (slow down time), to make effects like in Expedition 33. You'd need good animated battlers and spend time making the action sequences to make this stuff look good though.
